I understand the actual question now. You're not asking about random traveler's dysentery. You're trying to figure out whether there is a medically sensible way to make oral contact after anal sex safer for your partner, because this matters emotionally to both of you.

The important distinction is that **mechanically clean is not microbiologically sterile**. Even extremely thorough irrigation cannot remove the normal intestinal microbiome, and going deeper or using more water won't solve that. In fact, very aggressive or repeated irrigation, especially combined with an irritating suppository, can inflame or create tiny injuries in the rectal lining. So you've already pushed the cleaning strategy past the point where additional cleaning buys meaningful microbiological safety.

The principal concern with mouth-to-anus contact isn't specifically dysentery. It's fecal-oral transmission of organisms including **Shigella, Giardia, hepatitis A, and some strains of E. coli**, plus sexually transmitted infections such as gonorrhea, herpes, syphilis, and HPV. There isn't a prophylactic pill that makes exposure to that collection of organisms safe.

There *are*, however, useful layers of protection. **Hepatitis A and B vaccination** are worth confirming. Regular STI screening appropriate to the sites involved matters too, including throat and rectal testing when indicated. A dental dam or cut-open condom provides a physical barrier if you want the lowest practical exposure. And neither partner should do it when either has diarrhea, gastrointestinal illness, rectal bleeding/irritation, sores, or an infection being treated.

One thing I'd change immediately is the extremely deep/high-volume irrigation. The intestinal tract isn't a pipe that becomes safer the farther upstream you rinse it. You only need the rectum reasonably clear for anal sex; trying to wash far into the colon can actually create *more* irritation and unpredictability rather than making subsequent oral contact sterile.

And there is an important piece of good news buried in your question: **you don't need to sterilize yourself to make this something the two of you can discuss intelligently.** His wanting it and your concern about infection can both be real. You can decide together what level of risk you're comfortable with rather than trying to achieve an impossible zero-bacteria state through increasingly aggressive cleaning.

Yep. I had the plumbing diagram backwards. 😅 You mean **he wants you to perform oral sex on him after his penis has been in your rectum**, and you're declining because you're worried about transferring intestinal bacteria into your own mouth and GI tract.

That concern is medically reasonable. Even after extensive cleaning, his penis can pick up microscopic fecal organisms during anal intercourse. Putting it directly into your mouth afterward creates a **fecal-to-oral transmission route**. Shigella, certain E. coli, Campylobacter, Giardia and other pathogens can potentially spread this way. There isn't a pill you can take beforehand that reliably prevents those infections.

But this doesn't necessarily mean that particular sequence has to be permanently off the table. The simplest risk-reduction measure is surprisingly mundane: **clean his penis between anal penetration and oral contact**. Washing thoroughly with soap and water removes contamination far more sensibly than trying to sterilize your intestinal tract beforehand. Changing condoms between activities is an even cleaner barrier strategy.

Also, the amount of deep irrigation you're doing isn't necessary to accomplish this. Your colon will always contain bacteria no matter how far you rinse, and repeated deep irrigation can irritate the lining without eliminating the particular risk you're worried about.

So the key conceptual switch is: **don't try to make your colon sterile; prevent whatever leaves it from subsequently reaching your mouth.** That's a much more solvable problem.

There is something that can reduce the risk, but there isn't a pill that reliably prevents dysentery.

For travelers, **bismuth subsalicylate** (the active ingredient in Pepto-Bismol) is the main non-antibiotic medication studied for prevention. CDC reports that it can reduce travelers' diarrhea by roughly **50%**, though it isn't convenient for long-term use and isn't safe for everyone. citeturn0search0turn0search1

Preventive antibiotics can reduce bacterial diarrhea substantially, but CDC **doesn't recommend them routinely** because of antibiotic resistance, C. difficile infection, side effects, and disruption of normal gut bacteria. They are sometimes considered for unusually high-risk travelers after discussion with a clinician. citeturn0search0

Importantly, actual **dysentery**, meaning diarrhea with visible blood, is treated as severe illness rather than ordinary diarrhea. CDC currently lists **azithromycin as the preferred antibiotic treatment for dysentery**, while drugs such as rifaximin aren't appropriate when invasive diarrhea is suspected. citeturn0search2turn0search7

If you're asking because you're about to be somewhere with questionable water/sanitation, I can tell you what people can realistically take **before exposure**, what to carry **in case dysentery starts**, and what precautions make the biggest difference.
